latin.677: Lata lege vitium innatum sese multo quam antea clarius prodidit, ac pessimorum fructuum copia redundavit. Sed imputatio primi peccati actualis tam latuit quam antea, nullo legis praecepto, nulla comminatione, nulla sententia declarata. Immo illa imputatio cum lege Mosaica stare non potest, ut, Deo bene favente, suo loco planum faciam. Frustra igitur Apostolus illam temporis circumscriptionem adhibuisset usque ad legem, si de eiusmodi peccato actuali unius hominis omnibus imputato quaestio fuisset.
latin.678: GAR. Non est verum peccati illius actualis Adae imputationem, & ante & post legem datam, obscuram; corruptionem autem innatam & ex Adamo propagatam, cognitam fuisse. Nam si de Gentibus loquaris extra Ecclesiam, & Dei foedere agentibus, aeque fuit ignotum utrumque: Si de fidelibus, & foederis gratiae diuturnis consortibus, aeque notum utrumque: Neque enim putandum est Paulum, cum omnes docuit in Adamo peccasse, novum aliquod dogma procudisse, quod sub veteri Testamento fuerit omnino inauditum & incognitum, &c.
latin.679: PLAC. Primum unde habet Vir doctus fidelibus veteris Testamenti aeque notum utrumque fuisse? Ex Scriptura? Cur locum non protulit? Ex traditione non scripta? Non igitur sufficiebat illis Scriptura; & ubi illa traditio? Ad Paulum frustra confugit: utrum enim illam imputationem antecedentem docuerit, necne, nunc quidem inter nos controvertitur; docuisse non probavit Vir doctus; Ego non docuisse iam aliquot argumentis probavi, & in eo sum ut probem.
latin.680: Deinde si aeque ante ac post legem notum fuit, cur Apostolus dixit usque ad legem? quorsum spectant illa verba? Certe si tam notum fuit ante legem, quam post legem, peccatum fuisse in mundo, non magis opus fuit probare, peccatum ante quam post legem in hominibus fuisse. Denique corruptionem innatam post legem, quam ante, notiorem fuisse, ex legis & testimoniis quibus demonstrari potest, & fine qui fuit patefacere peccatum, & experientia, ac diserto Apostoli testimonio peccatum non cognovi nisi per Legem, ita clarum est, ut mirum sit caecutisse Virum doctum in tanta luce. Subiungit aliquid Augustini ex lib. 15. de Civitate Dei cap. 27. quasi ille agnovisset imputationem illam antecedentem, sed frustra. Nam & male interpretatus est verba Dei Gen. xvii. 14. peribit anima illius de populo meo, quoniam testamentum meum dissipavit, ea enim de masculo infante accepit nimis duriter, & videtur Vir doctus per testamentum illud non foedus circumcisionis intelligere, sed legem latam Adamo: cum tamen nec haec unquam foedus aut testamentum dicatur, & manifestum sit illud debere intelligi. Deinde ideo vult Augustinus perire illum infantem, quia non est regeneratus: opponitur autem regeneratio corruptioni inhaerenti, quae habitualis est testamenti Dei dissipatio ab Adamo propagata, non autem imputationi.
latin.681: Tertium argumentum mihi suppeditant quae sequuntur apud Apostolum: peccatum non imputatur cum lex non est. Atqui lex non est secundum quam nobis imputetur peccatum actuale Adami. Ergo non imputatur nobis. Probo minorem: nam maior est Apostoli. Si qua eiusmodi lex esset, ea esset singularis illa de non edendo fructu arboris scientiae boni & mali. Atqui illa iam ab aliquot annorum millibus non est amplius, sublata e rerum natura illa arbore, aut nobis prorsus ignota, &, ut caeteras Dei creaturas, concessa. Ergo lex non est secundum quam nobis imputetur peccatum actuale Adami.
latin.682: Ac ut lex illa primum eiecto e paradiso homine, deinde ipso paradiso sublato, esse non desiisset, quemadmodum proculdubio desiit, tamen eam ut legales caeremoniae Dominus suo adventu abrogasset. Fuit enim interdictum illud ceremonialis quaedam lex libertatem arbitrii humani circa rem natura sua indifferentem circumscribens. Quemadmodum igitur non potest nobis imputari violatio legis ceremonialis quia non sumus sub lege, sic non potest nobis imputari violatio legis olim latae in paradiso terrestri, quoniam sub ea non sumus, ac iam olim abrogata est. Atque haec tria argumenta versus 13. mihi dedit, tibi nullum.

pass_a.677: Placeus: once the law was given, innate vice showed itself far more clearly and overflowed with worst fruits. But imputation of Adam’s first actual sin stayed as hidden as before—no precept, threat, or sentence declared it. Indeed that imputation cannot stand with Moses’ law (he will show later). So Paul would have used ‘until the law’ in vain if the question were one man’s actual sin imputed to all.
pass_a.678: Garissoles denies the obscurity claim: Adam’s actual-sin imputation was not obscure before or after the law, with innate corruption known. Outside the church both were unknown; among the faithful both were known. Paul teaching that all sinned in Adam did not forge a dogma unheard under the Old Testament.
pass_a.679: Placeus asks the source: how does the learned man know OT faithful knew both equally? From Scripture—why no text? From unwritten tradition—then Scripture was not enough, and where is that tradition? Fleeing to Paul fails: whether Paul taught antecedent imputation is the very dispute; the opponent has not proved he did; Placeus has already proved he did not, and will prove further.
pass_a.680: Next: if both were equally known before and after the law, why did Paul say until the law—what are those words for? If sin in the world was as plain before as after, proving the pre-law case was no more needed than the post-law case. And innate corruption was clearer after the law—from the law’s witnesses, from the end of making sin plain, from experience, and from Paul’s I did not know sin except through the Law—so clear that the learned man’s blindness in that light is strange. Dragging Augustine City of God 15.27 for antecedent imputation fails: Gen 17:14 is misread of a male infant; testament means circumcision’s covenant, not Adam’s law, which is never called testament. Augustine has the infant perish for lack of regeneration, which opposes inherent corruption as habitual covenant-breaking from Adam, not imputation.
pass_a.681: Third argument from what follows: sin is not imputed when there is no law. But there is no law by which Adam’s actual sin is imputed to us. Therefore it is not imputed. The major is Paul’s. If any such law existed, it was the singular ban on the tree of knowledge. That ban has not existed for millennia—the tree gone from nature, or wholly unknown to us and granted like other creatures. So no such law remains.
pass_a.682: Even if that ban had not ceased when man was cast out and paradise removed (as it surely did), the Lord would still have abrogated it at his coming as he did legal ceremonies. It was a ceremonial law fencing free choice about a naturally indifferent thing. As ceremonial breach cannot be imputed because we are not under that law, so neither can breach of the old paradise law—we are not under it, and it was long abrogated. These three arguments verse 13 gave Placeus; none for the opponent.

677: When the law was given, innate vice showed itself far more clearly than before, and overflowed with a wealth of the worst fruits.
But the imputation of the first actual sin stayed as hidden as before, declared by no precept of the law, by no threat, by no sentence.
Indeed that imputation cannot stand with the Mosaic law, as, God favoring, I will make plain in its place.
In vain, therefore, would the Apostle have used that circumscription of time, until the law, if the question had been about that sort of one man’s actual sin imputed to all.
678: GAR. It is not true that the imputation of that actual sin of Adam was obscure both before and after the law was given, and that innate corruption propagated from Adam was known.

For if you speak of the Gentiles outside the Church and living without God’s covenant, both were equally unknown; if of the faithful and long partners of the covenant of grace, both were equally known.
Nor is Paul to be thought, when he taught that all sinned in Adam, to have forged some new dogma that under the Old Testament was altogether unheard of and unknown, etc.
679: PLAC. First, from where does the learned man have it that both were equally known to the faithful of the Old Testament?
From Scripture? Why did he not produce a place?
From unwritten tradition? Then Scripture was not enough for them; and where is that tradition?

He flees to Paul in vain: for whether Paul taught that antecedent imputation or not is just what is now disputed between us; the learned man has not proved that he taught it; I have already proved by several arguments that he did not, and I am engaged in proving it.
680: Next, if it was equally known before and after the law, why did the Apostle say until the law? To what do those words look?
Surely if it was as well known before the law as after that there was sin in the world, there was no more need to prove that sin was in men before the law than after it.

Finally, that innate corruption was better known after the law than before—from the law and the testimonies by which it can be shown, from the end which was to make sin plain, from experience, and from the Apostle’s express witness, I did not know sin except through the Law—is so clear that it is strange the learned man was blind in so much light.
He adds something of Augustine from City of God book 15 chapter 27, as if Augustine had acknowledged that antecedent imputation—but in vain.

For he also badly interprets God’s words in Gen. 17:14, that soul shall be cut off from my people, because he has broken my covenant—taking them too harshly of a male infant—and the learned man seems to understand by that covenant not the covenant of circumcision but the law given to Adam: though this is never called a covenant or testament, and it is plain the former must be meant.

Next, Augustine wants that infant to perish because he is not regenerated: but regeneration is opposed to inherent corruption, which is the habitual breaking of God’s covenant propagated from Adam, not to imputation.
681: A third argument is supplied to me by what follows in the Apostle: sin is not imputed when there is no law.
But there is no law according to which Adam’s actual sin is imputed to us.
Therefore it is not imputed to us.
I prove the minor: for the major is the Apostle’s.
If there were any such law, it would be that singular one about not eating the fruit of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil.
But that for some thousands of years now is no more—that tree having been removed from the nature of things, or being wholly unknown to us and, like the other creatures of God, granted.
Therefore there is no law according to which Adam’s actual sin is imputed to us.
682: And even if that law had not ceased to be, first when man was cast out of paradise, then when paradise itself was taken away—as it no doubt did cease—still the Lord would have abrogated it at his coming, as he did the legal ceremonies.
For that ban was a kind of ceremonial law fencing the freedom of human choice about a thing indifferent by its own nature.

As, therefore, violation of a ceremonial law cannot be imputed to us because we are not under the law, so violation of the law once given in the earthly paradise cannot be imputed to us, since we are not under it, and it was long ago abrogated.
And these three arguments verse 13 gave me—and none to you.
